# manifest.tsv: what the stub libraries of the sysroot offer to the linker. build-stubs.sh makes the
# stubs from this file, imports.py writes and checks it, and ../README.md explains both.
# Tab-separated fields, one record per line, the records sorted in byte order (LC_ALL=C sort):
#   lib   path in the sysroot | install name | current version | compatibility version |
#         install names of the libraries it re-exports, separated by one space, in the order of
#   link  path in the sysroot | target of the symlink
#   sym   install name of the library | symbol | imported by | note
#         imported by: the labels of our binaries that import the symbol from that library, separated
#                      by one space, or - . imports.py rewrites this field from the binaries.
#         note:        - , or where a symbol that none of our binaries imports comes from and how
#                      it was confirmed. Written by hand; imports.py keeps it.
# A sym row needs an importer or a note. A lib row without sym rows is a library that our binaries
# The rule for adding a symbol: only after it was shown to exist in that library on iPhone OS 3.1.x,
#   1. Against the SDK that the developer supplies: link a binary that uses the symbol with IOS3_SDK
#      set to the real iPhoneOS3.1.2.sdk, then run "imports.py update" on it. The linker found the
#      symbol in the SDK's library, and the binary records which library that was. (The rows that
#      carry a note today were confirmed with the look-up such a link makes: each name comes from
#      our own objects and was looked up, yes or no, in the SDK's library.)
#   2. With a dlsym() probe on a device that runs iPhone OS 3.1.x: write the row by hand, with a note
#      that names the device, the OS version and the date.
# No name is ever copied from the export list of an SDK library.
